legal.headline: Transparency on trial: Mapping courts’ compliance with the RTI Act
legal.hook: Transparency on trial: Mapping courts’ compliance with the RTI Act
legal.summary: At a time when the RTI system is facing multiple challenges, the judiciary must set an example by staying true to the essence of the legislation.
legal.contextNote: The constitutional interplay between the Right to Information Act, 2005 and judicial autonomy hinges on Central Public Information Officer, Supreme Court v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2020), which declared the Chief Justice's office a public authority, and Chief Information Commissioner v. High Court of Gujarat (2020), which ruled that High Court Rules override RTI Act provisions for accessing judicial records. Despite statutory mandates under Section 4 for proactive disclosure, various High Courts maintain restrictive, non-uniform RTI rules and high application fees that limit access to administrative and case-level data. For in-house legal teams: (1) Discontinue reliance on RTI applications under Section 6 for sourcing pleadings or court records; apply directly under specific High Court Copying Rules to prevent summary procedural rejections. (2) Ensure trade secrets or sensitive corporate data submitted during litigation are protected by seeking explicit confidentiality ring orders under High Court Original Side Rules, rather than relying on RTI Section 8(1)(d) commercial confidence exemptions post-filing.

(1) In-house counsel should review ongoing cases where interim orders are in place to assess their logical consistency and potential vulnerability to challenge. (2) Counsel should prepare for possible appeals or modifications based on this ruling, ensuring that all interim orders comply with the logical standards set by the court. (3) Monitor the development of this legal principle in future cases to anticipate shifts in judicial expectations regarding interim relief.
